# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

## Revision 24 (keel-cloud spec 215, 2026-11-04)

The rows keel-e2e-eval spec 134's review moved (`specs/215-the-corpus-fits-the-cards/corpus-rewording.md`, Table 1), before -> after (rule):

- Importance: Guessing memory, GPUs and run time before submitting -> Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs (`imp-own`)
- Importance: Running out of the group's allocation -> Keeping within the group's GPU-hour allocation (`imp-backwards`, `imp-cause`)
- Current solution: Sized from past runs; it ran as planned -> Ran first time, sized about right (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle -> Ran, holding about twice what it used (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Doubled everything to be safe; much sat idle -> Ran, holding three times what it used (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Guessed low; it died and was resubmitted -> Failed partway and had to be resubmitted (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Copied an old script and hoped -> Never ran to the end (`cs-fail`, `cs-measure`)
- Compatibility: The job went through SLURM or Kubernetes as usual -> could run a monitoring agent on the job's node {asked: could your job have run with a monitoring agent on its node} (`cmp-settled`, `cmp-subject`)
- Compatibility: The source code sat on the cluster -> kept the job's source code on the cluster (`cmp-subject`)
- Compatibility: The job's code was written in Python -> wrote the job's code in Python (`cmp-subject`)
- Relative advantage: The job runs first time, no resubmits -> A job that runs to the end first time (`ra-one`)
- Purchase friction: Letting it read job scripts and source code -> *(dropped)* -- folded into *A security review of an agent on every node* (it is a part of that review); `items` 3 -> 2, the pick (0) unmoved (`pf-overlap`, `pf-object`)
- Purchase friction: A budget line for the department's pilot -> A budget line in the department's plan (`pf-offer`)

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The three answers raise genuinely different reasons — proof of recovered waste on our own cluster, a security veto on a code-reading node agent, and grant-funded budgets that can't take a monthly fee — so leaving each on its own is how an operator would read them, with no group they wrongly belong in.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three speak to what would change the price, so nothing junk was grouped.

founder.order_why: The flow mostly runs context, problem, idea, then who pays, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after the commitment screens (20-21), where my first step already led to a paid pilot, and 'How should operators answer?' (24) comes after the interviews are marked sent.
founder.asked_twice: 20 and 22: the first real step I'd want them to take (a two-week measurement, then a paid pilot) and 'Offer a pilot?' ask about the same pilot; 3 and 4 also carry the same question, though they may be one context form split across two screens.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The flow from waste to worth to budget to sign-off to security makes sense, but the 'One more thing' screen on what takes the time is wedged in before the last numbered question instead of following it, so the numbering feels broken.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 overlap: I answered 6 weeks to 3 months for the security review, and screen 7 asked again what would take that time, which for me is mostly the same security review.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Nothing asked how we size and schedule jobs today (SLURM or Kubernetes, existing tools or scripts for right-sizing requests), how many GPUs the cluster has, or whether researchers would actually accept changed memory, GPU and time requests. That last one decides whether the waste comes back at all.

screens.instead: What would Expanse be worth to you a month, per GPU? Under $5 · $5 to under $10 · $10 to under $25 · $25 to under $50 · $50 or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say (the bands placed around the founder's own per-GPU low)

screens.why1: Right after I named $10,000 to $25,000 a month, asking where that money would actually come from is the obvious next thing to ask a cluster operator who signs off on software.
screens.why2: Budget line, chargeback to the teams that use it, a grant: these are exactly how I already talk about funding the cluster.
screens.why3: I know where our cluster's money comes from (the ops budget, grant allocations, recharge to groups), so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The list covers my real sources, including grants and recharge, but for me paying from 'an existing budget line' at this size means cutting something else in it, so it overlaps with 'Taken from other spending'.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the Expanse name I was already shown on the idea card, and the band is the one I gave.
screens.why6: One short question pointing back to my price, then five short spoken options and one escape, all easy to hold on first hearing.
screens.why7: Five sources of money in the card's order, all on the one measure and readable after 'would', three for and two against so it can go either way, with 'I can't say' as the one escape apart.
screens.instead: You said about $10,000 to $25,000 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? An existing budget line, with room in it · Charged back to the groups that use it · A new budget line, signed off for it · A grant or outside funding · Cut from something else we pay for · I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after where the money would come from, asking whether I can sign off on that spend myself is the obvious next step in the buying decision.
screens.why2: Sign off, per cluster and a month are how I talk about spend, and I take it in on one read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I can approve on my own and what has to go up the chain for a cluster tool at this price.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone, to my boss, to a committee or procurement, to not my call, and I can't say covers the rest.
screens.why5: Department head reads like a university department rather than how a shared or national cluster is run, where I'd say my director or the head of research computing, so the role feels slightly imported.
screens.why6: One question of twenty words, the amount says easily, four short options I can hold, and a single escape said last.
screens.why7: All on the one measure of who has to agree; the four come in order from alone to someone else's call with the named role second; two count for and two against; I can't say sits apart.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $10,000 per cluster a month yourself, or would your director have to agree? I could sign off myself · My director would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking who signs off, it makes sense to ask what else stands between me and buying, and a security review is the obvious gate for anything that runs on every node of my cluster.
screens.why2: A security review of an agent on every node is exactly how I'd say it, and the time bands are plain.
screens.why3: I know how our security and infosec people handle a new daemon on compute nodes and roughly how long that takes, so I can answer from experience.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover the range, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a real answer if we already allow such agents, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It names Expanse and the agent from the idea card I already saw, and nothing else of the founder's pitch or terms leaks in.
screens.why6: Heard once, the stem is one question, the first step is four options I can hold, and the follow-up is a clean either-or.
screens.why7: Every option is on the one measure (how long the review takes), there are five bands with an edge at about 6 weeks plus 'It wouldn't be needed', it can be supported or refuted, and 'I can't tell' is the one escape, apart.

screens.why1: I just put the security review of a node agent at 6 weeks to 3 months, so asking what would eat that time is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It plays back my answer as I picked it, and 'what would take the time' is a plain question I can answer at once, though 'what would take that long' would read a bit more naturally.
screens.why3: I know exactly what drags: the security team's review of a privileged daemon on every node, change control on the scheduler, and procurement and contract terms.
screens.why4: A free-text box with no options.
screens.why5: Expanse is the idea I was shown on purpose, and nothing new about the founder's plan or own terms reaches me here.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, no symbols; the band '6 weeks to 3 months' says cleanly aloud.

screens.why1: After price, who signs off and how long security review would take, asking whether I'd actually try it on my cluster is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: Running a two-week measurement on the cluster is plain to me; 'waste' is blunter than I'd say, since I'd call it idle or unused allocation, but I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I'd let something run across my nodes for two weeks is my call and something I decide regularly.
screens.why4: Firm yes, soft yes, soft no and no cover it cleanly, and the yes names the actual step.
screens.why5: 'Waste measurement' reads like the founder's own label, and the screen doesn't say whether it's free or whether my job data leaves the cluster, which is what I'd actually be agreeing to.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's step in its own verb, the soft yes is 'Probably yes' as the card allows when there's no smaller step, the sides are balanced two and two, and there's no escape.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you run a free two-week measurement of unused GPU hours on the cluster, with the data staying on-site, or not? Yes, I'd run it · Probably yes · Probably not · No
